title: HTTP/1.1
subtitle: How a web request and its response are written down, framed and carried over a connection.
summary: RFC 9112 defines how HTTP/1.1 messages look on the wire: a start line, header lines, a blank line and an optional body, all sent as plain text over a reliable connection such as TCP. It also says how to tell where a message ends, how chunked transfer works, and when a connection stays open for the next request. The meaning of methods, status codes and headers lives in RFC 9110; this document is the syntax and plumbing underneath.

eli5.summary: HTTP/1.1 is the polite way a browser and a website write notes to each other: a first line that says what you want, a few labeled lines, a blank line, and then the message. It also says how to know where one note ends and how to keep passing notes without hanging up.

questions: what does an http request look like
what is the difference between content-length and transfer-encoding
how do persistent connections work in http
why does http/1.1 require a host header

tldr.problem: Clients, servers and proxies need to agree exactly where an HTTP message starts and ends, or they misread each other.
tldr.mechanism: Text messages made of a start line, header field lines, an empty line and a body, whose length is set by Content-Length, chunked coding or connection close, carried over connections that stay open by default.
tldr.outcome: It is the text-based wire format still spoken by a large part of the web, and its strict framing rules are a key defense against request smuggling.

today: HTTP/1.1 is still everywhere: it is what curl, many application servers, reverse proxies and embedded devices speak, and it is the fallback when a client and server do not agree on HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) or HTTP/3 (RFC 9114). Browsers typically use the newer versions where they can, but the same semantics from RFC 9110 sit on top of all three. Because HTTP/1.1 is human-readable, tools such as telnet, nc and Wireshark make it easy to inspect by hand.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 is defined by three documents together: this one, "HTTP Semantics" (RFC 9110) and "HTTP Caching" (RFC 9111). RFC 9112 covers only how those semantics are conveyed: the message syntax, framing and connection management. Its stated goal is to define the complete set of requirements for HTTP/1.1 message parsers and message-forwarding intermediaries.

It obsoletes the messaging parts of RFC 7230; the rest of RFC 7230 moved into RFC 9110. The document uses ABNF (RFC 5234) for its grammar and is part of the Internet Standard STD 99.

Where does the meaning live? What GET or a 404 means is in RFC 9110. This RFC only says how to write them down and where they end.
sections.eli5: Think of two pen pals. One document says what you are allowed to ask for, and this document says how to fold, label and mail the letter so the other side can read it without mixing up where one letter ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Message format
sections.content:
An HTTP/1.1 message is a start line followed by a CRLF, zero or more header field lines each ending in CRLF, an empty line, and an optional message body. A request and a response differ only in the start line and in how the body length is worked out.

A request line is method SP request-target SP HTTP-version, for example GET /where?q=now HTTP/1.1. A status line is HTTP-version SP status-code SP [ reason-phrase ], where the status code is exactly three digits. A client should ignore the reason phrase, because it is not a reliable channel for information.

A recipient must parse a message as a sequence of octets in an encoding that is a superset of US-ASCII, not as Unicode text, because string handling of invalid multibyte sequences creates security holes. A sender must not generate a bare CR, and a server should respond with 400 (Bad Request) to something that does not match the grammar. The version is the case-sensitive text HTTP/1.1.
sections.eli5: Every note starts with one line saying what you want (or how it went), then some labeled lines like "From:" and "Size:", then one empty line that means "now comes the actual message."

sections.title: Request targets and the Host header
sections.content:
The request-target says what the request is about. There are four forms. Origin-form (absolute-path [ "?" query ]) is the usual one when talking straight to a server, and an empty path is sent as /. Absolute-form is a full URI and is what a client sends to a proxy. Authority-form is just host:port and is used only for CONNECT. Asterisk-form is * and is used only for a server-wide OPTIONS request.

A client must send a Host header field in every HTTP/1.1 request, and a server must answer 400 (Bad Request) to a request that lacks one, or has more than one Host line or an invalid value. This is what lets one server and IP address host many sites.

When a request arrives in origin-form, the server rebuilds the full target URI itself: the scheme is https on a secured connection and http otherwise, the authority comes from Host, and the path and query come from the request-target.
sections.eli5: The first line says which page you want. Because one building can hold many shops, the "Host" line says which shop you mean.

sections.title: Header lines and message body length
sections.content:
A header field line is a case-insensitive name, a colon, optional whitespace, the value and optional trailing whitespace. No whitespace is allowed between the name and the colon: a server must reject such a request with 400 (Bad Request). Old-style line folding (obs-fold) is deprecated, and a sender must not generate it.

The hard part of HTTP/1.1 is knowing where the body ends. Section 6.3 gives a strict order of precedence. Responses to HEAD and any 1xx, 204 or 304 response never have a body. A successful response to CONNECT turns the connection into a tunnel. If both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length are present, Transfer-Encoding wins. If chunked is the final coding, the body is read chunk by chunk. A valid Content-Length gives the exact number of octets. A request with neither has no body. Only a response may be delimited by the server closing the connection.

A sender must not send Content-Length in a message that has Transfer-Encoding. A message with both may be an attempted smuggling attack and ought to be handled as an error.
sections.eli5: The receiver has to know when the note ends. The note can say "I am 500 letters long," or it can arrive in labeled pieces ending with an empty piece, or the sender can just hang up when finished.

sections.title: Chunked transfer coding
sections.content:
When the sender does not know the size of the content in advance, such as dynamically generated output, it can use the chunked transfer coding. The body becomes a series of chunks, each a hexadecimal size, an optional chunk extension and CRLF, then that many octets of data and CRLF. A chunk of size zero ends the data, optionally followed by a trailer section of extra header fields, and then an empty line.

Chunked lets the sender keep the connection persistent and lets the recipient know it has received everything. A recipient must be able to parse it, must expect very large hexadecimal numbers without integer overflow, and must ignore unrecognized chunk extensions. A message body that uses chunked is incomplete if the final zero-size chunk has not arrived.

Transfer-Encoding is a property of the message in transit, unlike Content-Encoding, which is a property of the representation. In Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked, the content is compressed and then chunked. Chunked must not be applied more than once, and in a request it must be the last coding applied (a response may instead be ended by closing the connection). The registered transfer codings are chunked, compress, deflate and gzip, plus the deprecated aliases x-compress and x-gzip.
sections.eli5: If you are telling a story and don't know how long it will be, you say it in pieces. Before each piece you say how big it is, and when you are done you say "zero."

sections.title: Connection management
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 assumes only a reliable transport with in-order delivery. The http scheme defaults to TCP port 80. Connections are persistent by default, so many requests and responses can share one connection. A "close" connection option in the Connection header ends this: a sender that intends to close sends Connection: close.

Because HTTP/1.1 has no request identifier, responses must come back in the same order as the requests. A client may pipeline requests (send several without waiting), and a server must answer in order. A user agent should not pipeline after a non-idempotent method until it has the final response. Slow responses therefore block those behind them, which is why clients open several connections, and the RFC tells them to be conservative in how many.

Closing carries a trap. If a server fully closes a TCP connection and then receives more data, its TCP stack sends a reset that may erase the client's unread input, so servers typically half-close first, keep reading, and then fully close.
sections.eli5: Hanging up after every sentence is slow, so by default you keep the phone line open. If you ask three questions at once, the answers must come back in the same order, so one slow answer holds up the rest.

sections.title: HTTP over TLS and incomplete messages
sections.content:
HTTP over TLS is simply HTTP messages sent as TLS application data. The client also acts as the TLS client: it opens a connection to the server, sends the ClientHello, and sends its first request only after the handshake finishes. The RFC registers the ALPN protocol ID http/1.1, the bytes 0x68 0x74 0x74 0x70 0x2f 0x31 0x2e 0x31.

TLS closure matters for framing. A close alert tells the receiver that no more data will arrive. An "incomplete close" (closing without waiting for the peer's alert) is a signal that data may have been truncated, so a client should treat as complete only responses for which it got the full Content-Length or the final zero-length chunk. A response delimited by closing is complete only if a valid closure alert was received. Clients must send a closure alert before closing the connection.

More generally, a client that receives an incomplete response must record it as incomplete.
sections.eli5: If a secret-code phone call just goes silent, you can't tell if the story was finished. So the speakers say a proper goodbye, and the listener checks whether the story had its ending.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
Section 11 is about the dangers of line-based, text-framed messages. Response splitting (also called CRLF injection) happens when an attacker gets encoded CR and LF characters into a response header, such as a Location value built from the request, so one response looks like two. On a persistent connection or through a shared cache, the attacker's fake second response may be accepted as the answer to a different request. The recommended defense is to allow only the core protocol library to write CR or LF in the header section.

Request smuggling uses differences in parsing between recipients, for example a front-end proxy and a back-end server that disagree on where a request ends, to hide extra requests inside an apparently harmless one. The RFC added stricter parsing requirements, especially for message framing, to reduce it. The strict rules above, such as rejecting whitespace before the colon and treating Transfer-Encoding plus Content-Length as an error, exist for this reason.

HTTP has no integrity or confidentiality of its own. It relies on the transport, which is why the https scheme matters; plain http gives no protection against modification.
sections.eli5: If a trickster can sneak a fake "end of note" into your note, the next person will think the trickster's words are a different, real note. So the rules for reading must be strict and the same for everyone.

viz.caption: Framing rules that blunt smuggling and splitting

items.title: Octets, not characters
items.text: Parse messages as bytes in a US-ASCII superset, never as Unicode strings.

items.title: No space before the colon
items.text: A server must reject such a request with 400 (Bad Request).

items.title: Transfer-Encoding wins
items.text: If both it and Content-Length appear, Content-Length is overridden (an intermediary must remove it), the message should be treated as an error, and a server must close the connection after responding.

items.title: Only the core library writes CRLF
items.text: Keep applications away from the raw protocol stream so they cannot inject line breaks.
